transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ellen Park (Obsidian Head of ML), Ravi Shah (Obsidian CTO), Marta Lopez (Platform Eng)

Summary:
- Discovery focused on model selection across Redwood Hosted / Dedicated / Private options; primary concerns: context length, multilingual performance, tool-calling/function-calling, and security/compliance.
- Obsidian has a mixed workload: long-form docs (20k-60k tokens), multilingual support (EN, ES, FR, DE, JP), and tool-calling for internal data lookups.
- Key asks: recommendations for open models that support 32k+ context, guidance on cost/latency tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated), and plan to run benchmarks for hallucination/precision on multi-lingual prompts.

Topics:
- Current stack & constraints
- Context window requirements (32k vs 64k)
- Multilingual accuracy and tokenization concerns
- Tool-calling and structured output support
- Deployment options: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (security, KMS, SSO)
- Benchmark plan and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and Diego our SE will lead the model/infra part.
[00:12] Ellen: Hi, Ellen Park at Obsidian, I run the ML team, we mostly ingest long docs from research partners.
[00:20] Ravi: Ravi Shah, CTO, I'll focus on infra and security questions.
[00:25] Marta: Marta Lopez, platform eng, I'll help with any sample data we need.
[00:32] Diego: Great, thanks. Quick agenda — model selection for hosted/dedicated/private, context length, multilingual, and tool-calling. Is that right Ellen?
[00:40] Ellen: Yep, that's it. We'll also want to understand what open models you recommend and how much of a gap there is versus closed models for our use cases.

[02:05] Diego: To start, can you summarize current production usage? token distributions, typical request sizes?
[02:15] Ellen: Most is long; about 60% of our queries need >8k tokens, roughly 30% hit 20k-35k, and we have a small amount, like 5%, hitting 50k+ when we do whole-article summarization. Average languages are English 70%, Spanish 10%, French 8%, German 7%, Japanese 5% — numbers overlap cause some docs are bilingual.

[04:30] Maya: Great, that pushes us to consider models with 32k or 64k context. For open models, Mistral and Llama-3 variants are common picks; Redwood also supports trimmed/quantized variants to optimize latency/cost.
[04:52] Ravi: What about tool-calling? We need function calls to internal microservices and to pull structured records — any caveats?
[05:04] Diego: We support streaming + function/tool calling across hosted and dedicated. The main difference: in Dedicated or Private you get more control over networking (VPC peering) and limited egress for calls to internal endpoints, so it's easier to do on-prem tool integrations with private endpoints. Hosted requires setting up secure tunnels or using our secure data connectors.

[07:20] Marta: On private endpoints — how does KMS and key management work? We use an HSM-backed KMS currently.
[07:30] Diego: For Private deploys we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. For Dedicated we offer KMS integration options and customer-managed keys. Hosted offers envelope encryption with Redwood-managed KMS by default, and customer-managed KMS for enterprise tiers. We'll share the SOC2/ISO docs.

[09:00] Ellen: Back to models — hallucination is a big worry. Which open models handle instruction-following + grounding best?
[09:12] Diego: From our benchmarks, Llama-3-instruct variants and Mistral-instruct-style models do well if you pair them with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and strong prompt engineering. Also prefix/KV caching helps for repeated contexts to reduce hallucination by keeping context consistent. Note: KV cache sometimes transcribed in our older docs as "KV cash" — minor aside, sorry.

[11:40] Ellen: For multilingual accuracy, we've seen a lot of variance. Any recommended models that are particularly good multi-lingual out of the box?
[11:52] Diego: Larger open models with multilingual pretraining — some Llama-3 and certain Mistral variants are better. But there's still a gap for low-resource languages. With Redwood you can host model ensembles or language-specialized models and route by language. There's a small latency cost for routing but it improves quality.

[13:30] Ravi: Latency/cost tradeoffs — can you give ballpark numbers for hosted vs dedicated for 32k context?
[13:42] Diego: Roughly: hosted (multi-tenant) latencies for 32k contexts on an open 70B-class quantized model can be in the 600-1200ms per token generation range depending on batching; cost per token is higher but zero infra ops for you. Dedicated reserved capacity brings down tail latency and unit cost because you control GPU affinity and batching; expect 30-50% lower cost per effective token and more predictable latency. Private/on-prem adds operational overhead but gives full data control and can be cost-competitive if you amortize hardware. We'll send a detailed pricing breakdown.

[16:15] Ellen: How about context windows beyond 32k? We might need 64k for some workflows. What's supported?
[16:23] Diego: We have runtime support for 64k contexts on certain model variants and GPU types. The tradeoffs are higher memory usage and increased latency. For long contexts we recommend: 1) segment + RAG to avoid sending the entire doc every request; 2) prefix caching for repeated prefixes; 3) if you truly need 64k full attention, use dedicated pools with GPUs that support large memory and our optimized kernels.

[18:50] Marta: Tool-calling again — we will call internal inventory microservice that returns JSON. Does Redwood support structured output and schema enforcement?
[19:00] Diego: Yes, we have structured output primitives and function calling; you can define JSON schema for the tools and the model will use function calls. We'll also provide hooks to validate outputs server-side and reject malformed responses. For high assurance you can run a lightweight verifier in the call path.

[21:30] Ellen: Any gotchas with tokenization across languages? We have mixed scripts in same doc.
[21:40] Diego: Mixed-script documents can blow up token counts due to subword tokenization differences. We advise sampling your corpus and running a tokenization pass; Marta, if you can provide a couple of representative files we can include that in the benchmark to estimate real token distribution.

[23:20] Maya: On the enterprise control plane: RBAC, audit logs — what does Redwood provide for Dedicated and Private?
[23:30] Diego: RBAC is available across all tiers; Dedicated and Private give you access to richer audit logs and longer retention. For Private we can pipeline logs into your SIEM. We also provide request-level tracing for debugging.

[25:55] Ravi: Security review — we need to see SOC 2, ISO 27001 and data residency commitments. Also networking diagrams for VPC peering.
[26:10] Maya: We'll share the security/compliance pack and a high-level VPC diagram. For Hosted we have regional controls and enterprise agreements for data residency; Dedicated and Private give stronger guarantees.

[28:40] Ellen: Benchmark plan — we'd like to validate hallucination/error rates, latency, and cost across languages and context sizes.
[28:52] Diego: Proposed plan: run a 48-hour hosted sandbox benchmark with 3 model families (Llama-3-variants, Mistral-instruct, and a quantized Llama-3-light) across 8k, 32k, and one 64k scenario. We'll measure latency, tokens/cost, hallucination (using your ground truth checks), and function-calling fidelity. We'll also do a Dedicated run if you want to test reserved capacity.

[31:05] Marta: For the sandbox test, what do you need from us?
[31:12] Diego: Samples: 200 representative prompts, 50 long documents (20-60k tokens), language labels, and example functions / tool schemas. Also, credentials for any internal test endpoints if we test tool-calls against your services (we can use a secure tunnel).

[33:40] Ellen: If we start with Hosted sandbox and then move to Dedicated, what's the onboarding time and migration friction?
[33:52] Maya: Onboarding to Hosted sandbox is immediate — you get API keys and access. Moving to Dedicated usually takes 2-6 weeks depending on capacity and contract; we handle model pinning and rollout. Private/on-prem can be months depending on infra.

[36:15] Ravi: Any limits on function call complexity? We have nested JSONs and up to 5 sequential calls in a session.
[36:28] Diego: We handle nested JSON and multiple sequential calls; you may want to design idempotent endpoints. Note that each function call adds to token usage and latency — we'll show tradeoffs in the benchmark.

[38:00] Ellen: A quick question on quantization — does it materially impact multilingual fidelity?
[38:10] Diego: For many models, 8-bit quantization is fine for general quality but can slightly reduce fidelity for nuanced multilingual outputs. We recommend testing quantized variants in the benchmark, and for critical cases keep a float16 or 4-bit tuned variant if you need precision.

[40:20] Maya: Anything else on the architecture side?
[40:30] Ravi: We'll need support for SSO/SAML and SCIM for user provisioning.
[40:36] Maya: Enterprise tiers include SSO/SAML and SCIM; we'll include setup guide in the pack.

[42:12] Ellen: Ok, recap: send pricing/hosted vs dedicated comparison, security docs, benchmark plan; we'll provide sample data and decide timeline after the benchmark results.

[42:30] Maya: Yep — Diego will own the benchmark plan and I'll send pricing/security.

[43:05] Diego: I'll draft a 48-hour sandbox run and list required artifacts; also include a first-pass set of prompts derived from typical research summaries.

[44:00] Ellen: Great, thanks everyone. Looking forward to the benchmark.

[44:12] Maya: Thanks — we'll target sending materials by Friday.

[44:20] Ravi: Thanks all.

[44:25] (call ends)

Notes: A few transcription artifacts present (names sometimes shortened, minor mis-hear). References to KV cache, prefix caching, and quantization were discussed; Redwood to provide reference docs and benchmark plan.
